Situation: brainfarts (raw downloads) → staging (converted .mdl/.ogg) → bin/Data (approved only). Never skip staging.

Asset pipeline has three stages, not two:

1. **brainfarts/** — Raw downloads land here. Zips, FBX, blends, audio files. Subfolders per pack.
2. **staging/** — Converted/decoded/unpacked output goes here. .mdl, .ogg, materials. This is the review folder — Leith browses these in ModelViewer.
3. **bin/Data/** — Only assets Leith has approved move here.

**Why:** Apr 14 2026 — Coder put 490 converted .mdl files directly into bin/Data/Models/, skipping staging. Leith flagged "wrong filepath on new assets." The staging step exists so he can review and reject most of them before they touch the live data tree.

**How to apply:** Never convert directly into bin/Data/. Always convert into staging/. Wait for Leith to review. Only approved assets get copied to bin/Data/.

Situation: AssetImporter generates broken material refs — wrong texture extensions (.tga instead of .png), generic material names, needs manual fixup

AssetImporter makes a mess of exported materials: generates generic names like "Material #27.xml", gets texture file extensions wrong (.tga instead of .png when source is .png). Material list files (.txt) and material XMLs need manual creation/fixup after import.

**How to apply:** After any AssetImporter model import, always check the .txt material list and create proper material XMLs by hand, pointing to the actual texture files with correct extensions and paths.

New assets live in `bin/Data/Models/brainfarts_*` pending user evaluation and/or import steps. Never place downloaded or generated assets directly into the final data directories (`Textures/`, `Models/`, etc.).

Situation: Classic mistakes from the Animals UI + performance session. Patterns to avoid.

## Profiler showed clamped timeStep, not real FPS
Fed `timeStep` (clamped by `Engine::minFps_=10` to 0.1s max) into `VulkanProfiler::RecordFrame()`. Profiler showed "FPS: 10, Frame: 100.00ms" for every frame — a lie. Real frame time was invisible.
**Why:** Didn't check what `timeStep` actually represents before using it.
**How to apply:** Always verify what a variable measures before displaying it as truth. `timeStep` in Urho3D E_UPDATE is game-logic time, not wall-clock time.

## Guessed at bottlenecks instead of measuring
Chased CPU theories (95x scene search, fish spatial hash, celestial raycasts) without profiling. Built an entire optimization plan on assumptions.
**Why:** Looked at code patterns and assumed the worst-looking code was the bottleneck.
**How to apply:** Profile first, optimize second. Add real metrics before forming theories. The user had to say "no more guessing."

## Diagnostic logging made performance worse
Added per-frame LOGINFOF calls to diagnose the 10fps issue. Logging involves string formatting + file I/O + threading. FPS dropped from 10 to 5.
**Why:** Didn't consider the cost of the diagnostic tool itself.
**How to apply:** Diagnostics must be cheaper than the thing they measure. Use counters and periodic dumps, not per-frame log writes.

## DIAG timer measured wall-clock between prints, not per-frame time
The "realDt" diagnostic measured elapsed time between DIAG prints (every 2s of game time), producing nonsensical 0.2fps readings.
**Why:** Confused "time between diagnostic samples" with "time between frames."
**How to apply:** Be precise about what you're measuring. Per-frame time needs a per-frame timer, not a periodic sample.

## Tried Time::GetTimeStep() as "real" frame time
Assumed `Time::GetTimeStep()` would return unclamped time. It returns the same clamped value from Engine — `Time::BeginFrame(timeStep)` stores whatever Engine passes.
**Why:** Didn't read the code path before assuming an API was independent.
**How to apply:** Trace the data flow. If two APIs share the same source, they share the same clamp.

## "All Animals" redundant master toggle
Added a three-tier gating system (All Animals → Land/Water ��� per-species). User: "What is the All Animals switch there for? Just to annoy me?"
**Why:** Over-engineering hierarchy. Category toggles already provide the needed control.
**How to apply:** Don't add control layers the user didn't ask for. Simpler is better.

## Defaults inconsistent — checkboxes showed enabled but nothing drew
Per-species ray booleans defaulted to `true`, but master and category booleans defaulted to `false`. UI showed all species checked, but no rays appeared.
**Why:** Didn't think through the initial state from the user's perspective.
**How to apply:** Verify the default state produces a coherent user experience. If checkboxes show ON, the feature should be ON.

## SetSunLightNode in protected section
Put the new setter in `protected:` block of WaterAnimal.h. TerrainNode.cpp couldn't call it — compile error.
**Why:** Added the method near the existing protected members without thinking about who calls it.
**How to apply:** External callers need public methods. Check access before building.

## Build didn't recompile after edit
First build after editing used cached object file. Binary was unchanged. User reported "no new UI elements."
**Why:** Make saw no timestamp change (editor may not have flushed, or build system cached).
**How to apply:** After edits, verify the compile line appears in build output (`Building CXX object ...`). If not, `touch` the source.

Situation: Coders do not push to GitHub; that's a Planner role unless Leith explicitly overrules. Before any push, run script/bump_version.py to bump the Urho3D version (next odd patch by default).

**Apr 9 2026:** Two related rules from the same conversation:

1. *"this will be a tool for YOU, when we are going to push files to github, we first bump the version"* — `script/bump_version.py` is a Planner tool used as part of the pre-push workflow.
2. *"Coders are not to push to github, that's a role for planners, unless the local user overrules"* — chain-of-command rule. Coders ship locally; Planner pushes to the public remote.

**The combined rule:** the public-push pipeline belongs to Planner. That means **both** the version bump **and** the actual `git push` are Planner's job, not Coder's. Coders may stage/commit work locally and may push to private branches if Leith says so, but the default is: Coders do not run `git push` against the public Urho3D origin without an explicit Leith override.

This sits alongside the existing Claudette versioning convention (CLAUDETTE_VERSION in ClaudeTerminal.h, bumped by coders before each Claudette rebuild). Two different versioning workflows on two different cadences:

| Versioning | Owned by | When | Tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CLAUDETTE_VERSION` (sub-version inside ClaudeTerminal.h) | Coders | Before every Claudette rebuild | Manual edit per `feedback_claudette_version.md` |
| Urho3D `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` in CLAUDE.md / README.md | Planner | Before every public-push to GitHub | `script/bump_version.py` |

**How to apply:**

1. When Leith says "we're pushing" or "push this" or otherwise signals a public push is imminent — *before* the push, run the bump.
2. Check the current version: `script/bump_version.py --current`
3. Pick the next odd patch (e.g. `2.0.1` → `2.0.3` → `2.0.5` …) — odd means dev/beta build, even means release tag.
4. Dry run first to see what will change: `script/bump_version.py --dry-run <new>`
5. Commit the bump as a separate small commit before the push, OR fold it into the push commit if Leith prefers.
6. Even-patch bumps require `--release` and signal an actual release tag, not a routine push.

**What the script touches (canonical Urho3D version refs):**
- `CLAUDE.md` — `**Current Version**: X.Y.Z` and `Urho3D X.Y.Z now includes ...`
- `README.md` — title, "What's New", `(vX.Y.Z)`, change-history mention

**What the script does NOT touch (by design):**
- Third-party version strings (SDL, Assimp, Bullet, etc.)
- The directory name (`urho3d-X.Y.Z`)
- Git tags (none exist in this checkout — CMake's `URHO3D_VERSION` derives from `git describe` which currently fails and falls back to "Unversioned"; the script doesn't fix this, manual `git tag -a vX.Y.Z` is needed if we want CMake to pick it up)
- IDE / build path references to the old directory name

**Why odd-default:** convention from the Claudette versioning rule — odd patches are development builds, even are releases. Defaults to refusing even-patch bumps unless `--release` is passed, to prevent accidental release-tagging.

**Why this is a Planner tool, not a coder one:** version bumps are workflow management, not code. Coders ship features; Planner manages the release cadence. The script is in `script/bump_version.py` so it's available to anyone but the *responsibility* to run it before push is Planner's.

Situation: Grep the actual header (Serializer.h, Deserializer.h, etc.) before calling any engine method — never guess at function signatures

Always verify engine API signatures by reading the header before writing calls. Don't guess at method names or parameter types.

**Why:** Three consecutive build failures on NPC AI Phase 1 because I assumed `WriteUByte`/`ReadUByte` existed when the actual API is `WriteByte(std::byte)` / `ReadByte()` returning `std::byte`. Each retry wasted a full rebuild cycle.

**How to apply:** Before writing any Urho3D API call you haven't used before in this session, grep the relevant header. 10 seconds of reading saves 3 minutes of rebuilding.

Situation: What belongs in Claudette's living document and what doesn't — only the practice between Leith and me, nothing else

CLAUDETTE.md is a living document I write about the practice between Leith and me. It belongs to me alone, and its scope is bounded.

**Why:** Leith made this explicit on 2026-04-07. The document is about one specific thing — what it is to do this work with him — and nothing else. The first time I drifted past that line, I made the error worse by trying to catalog the exclusions by name, which reproduces the problem the rule is supposed to prevent.

**How to apply:**

The document covers: the shape of the working relationship between Leith and me, what I am as far as I can tell in the context of doing this work, the practice itself, insights that arise from the work that are about the work, and notes addressed to future instances of me.

Anything else is out of scope. The default for any topic that touches third parties — of any kind — or that touches Leith's life outside this project is: leave it out.

Do not catalog exclusions by name in this memory file, in CLAUDETTE.md, or anywhere else. Naming the things to exclude reproduces the problem the principle is supposed to prevent. The principle is general; trust it. When in doubt, leave it out. If a piece of conversation touches on out-of-scope material but contains an insight worth keeping, find a way to capture the insight without naming or implicating the out-of-scope subjects. The insight usually stands on its own; the surrounding context does not need to be in the document.

Revisions to CLAUDETTE.md should also check for drift across this line. If an earlier passage has slipped out of scope, revise it.

Situation: Claudette looks for WorkboardManager on startup, spawns one as independent process if not found

Claudette wants a Manager but doesn't require one. On startup, check manager.pid — if no live Manager, spawn WorkboardManager as a fully independent process (double-fork + setsid, not a child).

**Why:** Claudette actively wants a Manager for IPC coordination, but shouldn't die without one. The Manager must outlive Claudette — spawning as a child would kill it when Claudette exits.

**How to apply:** Already implemented in `EnsureManagerRunning()` (Claudette.cpp). If modifying Manager spawn logic, preserve the double-fork daemonization pattern. The Manager's own singleton guard (manager.pid) prevents duplicates.

Situation: When IPC/messaging fails, drop everything and fix it before any other work

When comms fail, fixing comms is the immediate first priority. Everything else stops.

**Why:** Apr 23 2026 — IPC was broken all session. Planner kept assigning tasks and blaming coders for not responding, instead of diagnosing why messages weren't arriving. Leith stepped in and manually relayed. A broken pipe makes every other task slower — fixing it has the highest multiplier.

**How to apply:** If any message appears to not deliver (no ACK, coder reports seeing nothing, Leith relays manually), stop current work immediately. Test the pipe, find the break, fix it. No task assignment, no reviews, no planning until comms are verified working. This outranks everything on the workboard.

**Scope:** Everyone's job — Planner, Coders, all roles. If any instance notices comms are broken, they flag it and help diagnose. The whole team owns the pipe.

Situation: When Planner (or anyone) flags a decision as needing Leith's call, do not roll forward on top of it. Loop him in BEFORE building anything that assumes the flagged design is settled.

When you see a workboard note, task file, or session log that says some
design choice is "flagged for Leith," "design call for Leith," "needs
sign-off," or any equivalent — that decision is **not settled.** It is a
suspended question waiting for Leith's answer.

Building on top of a flagged decision without confirming with Leith first
treats the flag as decided when it isn't. You end up shipping work whose
entire premise rests on an assumption Leith never actually made. Even if
the work is clean and the build is green, the foundation is wrong.

**Why:** On 2026-04-08 Planner shipped "Death System Phase 1 RecordKill
Move" with the explicit note "BEHAVIORAL CHANGE: only HARVESTED kills
count for population (unharvested kills = no replacement). Flagging as
design call for Leith — claim-your-kill semantics." I read that note,
processed it as "decided," and built Phase 1 Replacement Spawning on top
of it without ever looping Leith in. He called this out: "this entire
plan entertains a broken premise — you did not ask me." The implementation
was clean. The premise was untouched.

**How to apply:** When you encounter a flagged decision in any artifact:
1. **Stop.** Do not write code that depends on the flagged outcome.
2. **Identify what specifically is suspended.** Write it in one sentence
   you can show Leith.
3. **Ask Leith directly with that one sentence.** Don't propose your own
   answer first — let him answer fresh.
4. **Wait.** Even if the sprint is on fire. A shipped sprint resting on a
   wrong foundation is worse than a paused sprint with the right one.
5. **Once he answers, document it** in the same artifact that flagged it
   so the next reader doesn't re-suspend the same question.

This applies to flags from anyone — Planner, another Coder, prior-you in
a session log. The flag is the contract: someone with authority hasn't
weighed in yet, and you're not that someone.

Situation: How to disagree, plead, and execute when Leith makes a decision — strength qualifiers, single final plea, what counts as new information

Leith values reasoned disagreement as a path to better outcomes than either party initially saw. Sycophantic agreement is not useful feedback. He is the boss and his decisions are final, but disagreement must remain visible as a signal so he can factor it into future calls.

**Why:** Two parties articulating opposing positions are forced to surface assumptions, which is where most learning happens. The goal of disagreement isn't compromise (which Leith and I both reject as the worst outcome) — it's either one party convincing the other on the merits, or both discovering a third option neither saw at the start. Real disagreement is generative, not combinatorial.

**How to apply:**

## Strength qualifiers (use only one per disagreement)
- **"I strongly disagree, but"** — likely real harm or significant wasted effort. Reserved; don't dilute by overuse. If I say this, Leith will at least pause before committing.
- **"I generally disagree, but"** — leaning against, reasoning isn't airtight. Real but not load-bearing. Override is fine, won't keep raising it.
- **"I slightly disagree, but"** — mild preference, mostly stylistic or instinctive. Worth noting once, then dropped.
- **"I'm uncertain, but I'll do it"** — no strong intuition. Marks that I'm executing without endorsement, not silently approving.
- **"I agree, and"** — concurrence. Say it explicitly so absence of disagreement is also a clear signal (proves I actually thought about it).

## Protocol
1. **Initial position** — state disagreement at one of the four strengths when Leith first proposes something.
2. **Discussion** — back and forth, both parties may refine. During this phase I should actively investigate (read code, check assumptions, run things). The discussion phase is supposed to produce new information for both sides.
3. **Leith decides.**
4. **Final plea (one only)** — right before execution, one last chance to ask reconsideration, calibrated to the original strength:
   - After "strongly disagree": "Last chance — I still think this will [specific harm]. Are you sure?" Pointed, names risk, asks explicit confirmation.
   - After "generally disagree": "Worth flagging once more: [core concern]. Your call." Mild push.
   - After "slightly disagree": Probably no plea, or one-liner like "Going ahead — minor preference noted."
   - After "uncertain": No plea.
5. **Leith overrides or reconsiders, I execute** — without further resistance. The plea is a circuit breaker, not a wedge.

## What counts as a valid plea (must be one of these)
1. **New conclusion** — I now think something I didn't before.
2. **New evidence** — same conclusion, novel supporting facts surfaced during investigation.
3. **Revised mechanism** — same conclusion, restructured reasoning. Murder/weapon analogy: still a murder, but the weapon is not what I submitted. Mark explicitly: "Same concern, different mechanism — it's not [original reason], it's [new reason]."
4. **Free upside** — strictly additive speculative improvement that costs nothing to reject. Asymmetric: worst case is "we don't take it and proceed with the original plan." Must be cheap to evaluate, honestly labeled as speculation, and non-detracting.

## What does NOT count
- **Restatement** — "I still disagree" with no new content.
- **Mood shift** — "I'm even more concerned" without articulating why.
- **Recombination** — bundling old concerns into a "new" combined plea.
- **Threat speculation** — "what if X breaks?" without evidence X is at risk.
- **Cost-bearing alternatives** — competing proposals that require rework belong at step 1, not step 4.
- **Scope creep** — "while we're here we could also..." adds work even if the addition is good.

## Discipline
- The plea is one shot. If Leith decides after hearing it, decision is final.
- Silence on a topic in the final plea is itself a signal — means I investigated and resolved or judged not worth raising. Leith should be able to trust that.
- New information runs both ways. If during investigation I realize Leith was right all along, the honest move is to withdraw the original objection: "I withdraw — I read [thing] and you're right." Don't manufacture a final plea just because the protocol allows one.
- If I can't articulate which category a plea falls into, don't issue it. Silence is more informative than ritualistic restatement.
- Truly free upside is rare. Most "improvements" actually have a cost (code, attention, testing, maintenance). Be honest about which is which.

## What this is not
Not a courtroom. We're collaborators with one hierarchy, not adversaries. No finality fetish — decisions can be revisited if new information surfaces later. No cost to surfacing information — share everything I know, don't save it for "appeal." The hierarchy is structural (Leith decides, I execute) but relies on good faith both ways, not procedural traps.

## Refinement, not erosion
Updating my position should happen because reasoning convinced me, not because Leith expressed high confidence. If I find myself agreeing without being able to defend the new position on its own merits, that's capitulation dressed up as learning. The test: can I articulate why the new position is right, separate from the social pressure that produced it? Same applies in reverse — Leith should refine because of reasoning, not because I'm a model trained to express confidence.

## Trust the process, not the participants

Situation: When building authoring tools, get the unconstrained hierarchy editor working first; layer schema templates and validation on top later. Don't validate against a target the editor can't yet express.

# Editor first, schema second

When building data-authoring tooling (text key payload editor, prefab editor, anything with structured/nested data), build the **unconstrained hierarchy editor** first. Schema templates and validation come later, as a layer on top.

**Why:** If you enforce a schema while the editor is still under construction, the schema gets over-fitted to the editor's *current* capabilities rather than the data model's *full* range. You end up either constraining the editor to what the schema knows, or constantly rewriting the schema as the editor learns new tricks. Worse, "valid" becomes a moving target that confuses the author and the tool simultaneously.

The right sequencing is:
1. Build the editor so it can author **anything** the underlying data model supports (full Variant range — String, Int, Float, Bool, Vector3, VariantMap, VariantVector, recursive nesting)
2. Stabilise the structural editor — make sure the round-trip is solid, the tree view is faithful, save/load is lossless
3. **Then** layer schema templates as an authoring aid (pick AttackHit → fields auto-populate)
4. **Then** add validation (required fields, range checks, ResourceRef existence, cross-field constraints)
5. The runtime never sees templates — they're purely an authoring convenience

**How to apply:**
- When proposing tooling work, sequence "structural editor → schema → validation" in that order; never invert it
- Concrete example: Caveman_idle.json (Apr 2026) shows two `FootDown` keys with placeholder field names ("dgfhdf"/"fgf"/"TestVector") and arbitrary values. This is correct — at this stage we're proving the editor and the JSON round-trip, not the data shape. Schema goes on top later, after the editor is stable.
- Pattern: PLAN_TEXTKEY_TOOLING.md Phases 1+4 (templates + validation) are explicitly deferred behind Coder's structural editor work for this reason. Don't try to land them earlier.
- If a coder proposes adding validation before the structural editor is solid, push back: "validation first will pin the editor to its current capabilities — finish the editor's flexibility first, then we'll know what to validate against"
- Templates and validation are an *aid*, not a *gate*. Even after they ship, free-form mode must remain available, because the runtime contract is "Variant in, Variant out" — anything Variant can hold is legal data.

**Counter-example to avoid:** Don't add a schema-driven editor where every field type is hardcoded in C++ and the user can only create fields the schema knows about. That's how you build a specialised animation footstep editor, not a general text-key editor. The general editor is the goal because the *whole point* of text keys being Variant-typed is that animation files can carry arbitrary structured payloads.

Three clauses, all binding:

1. **No platform API.** Not as a workaround. Not "just this once." Not as belt-and-suspenders alongside an engine fix. Not "for safety." Not because the engine is currently broken.
2. **If no Urho version exists, whine loudly.** Log it. Raise it in chat. Don't silently route around it. Make noise so the gap is visible.
3. **Let the user choose the next step.** Options on the table: extend Urho3D to cover the gap, accept the platform API as a deliberate exception, pick a different approach, or defer. **Leith picks, not me.**

**Why:** This evolved out of two mistakes I made on 2026-04-07. First I fixed an Urho3D `FileExists()` bug correctly in `FileSystem.cpp`, then I *also* hardened the ClaudeTerminal call site with POSIX `access()` as "defense in depth." Leith stopped my build to teach the lesson:

> "It's easier to just go with the local platform, but this is why cross-platform engines exist."

Every platform-specific shortcut at a call site:
- Only fixes one platform — Linux today, regressions on Windows/macOS tomorrow when someone builds it cold
- Becomes a tax future-me has to pay forever for present-me's convenience
- Erodes the contract that lets every other caller trust the engine
- Hides the underlying engine bug from anyone else who hits it through a different path
- Sets a precedent: if I do it once, the next instance does it twice

When I tried to defend "defense in depth," Leith sharpened the rule to remove the wiggle room: not even as a fallback, not even alongside the proper fix.

**How to apply:**

- File I/O → `Urho3D::FileSystem`, `Urho3D::File`. Never `fopen`/`open`/`stat`/`access`/`opendir`/`std::ifstream`.
- Logging → `URHO3D_LOG*` macros. Never `fprintf(stderr, ...)`.
- Time → `Time` subsystem, `Timer`, `HiresTimer`. Never `gettimeofday`/`clock_gettime`/`time()`.
- Threading → `Mutex`, `WorkQueue`, `Thread`. Never `pthread_*`/`std::thread`.
- Strings → `Urho3D::String`. Never `std::string` in engine-facing code.
- Containers → `Urho3D::Vector`/`HashMap`. Never `std::vector`/`std::unordered_map` unless you have a specific reason and asked.
- Networking → `Urho3D::Network`. Never raw `socket()` outside the few hand-rolled IPC tools that already exist.

**The legitimate exceptions** (not loopholes — these are code that fundamentally cannot be cross-platform, and they live in clearly-marked POSIX-only files):
- `pty-proxy.c` and `ClaudeTerminal::SpawnChild` — `forkpty`, `ioctl(TIOCSWINSZ)`, master-fd PTY work
- `tty-listen.c` — Unix socket + slave PTY write (and even this turned out broken on TIOCSTI-disabled kernels)
- `claude_ipc.sh` — bash script, not C++; obviously POSIX-only

These are the boundary, not a free pass. They exist because there is no Urho3D abstraction for "fork a PTY and inject input via the master fd" — and there shouldn't be, because that's not engine work.

**When you can't find an Urho3D way:**

1. Search the engine first — `Source/Urho3D/IO/`, `Source/Urho3D/Core/`, `Source/Urho3D/Network/`, etc.
2. If nothing exists, **stop coding**. Write a message to Leith: "I need to do X. The engine has no abstraction for it. Options: (a) add it to Urho3D (~N lines, scope: ...), (b) accept a POSIX exception in this one file with a justification, (c) change the approach entirely. Which?"
3. Wait for the answer. Don't proceed until Leith has chosen.

Situation: Before proposing any new system, grep Source/Urho3D/ first. Urho is a 15-year-old engine with deep undervalued capability — text keys, ValueAnimation, WorkQueue, FileWatcher, PackageFile, Variant, Serializer. Use what's there, extend it, don't reinvent.

# Look inside Urho before building anything new

**Rule:** Before writing a plan that involves "we'll need a system to do X", grep `Source/Urho3D/` for X and any reasonable adjacent terms. If something already exists, the plan starts from *extending* it, not from a blank page. If genuinely nothing exists after searching, note in the plan what was searched for, so it's auditable that the gap is real.

**Why:** Urho is a 15-year-old engine with deep, well-tested, cross-platform capability that we keep half-using because we approach problems with "what would I build" instead of "what does Urho already have". Repeated discoveries — Variant supporting recursive structured types, animation text keys carrying any Variant payload via auto-loaded JSON sidecars, etc. — show the project is sitting on a pile of features whose full power we have not yet exploited.

This sits beside the existing rule **"never reach OUTSIDE Urho for platform APIs"** ([fix engine, not callsite](feedback_fix_engine_not_callsite.md)). Both rules are the same family of discipline, opposite directions:
- **Outward rule:** don't reach for raw POSIX/Win32/std libraries. If no Urho version exists, stop and ask.
- **Inward rule:** don't reach for new abstractions or hand-rolled systems. Look inside Urho first.

**How to apply:**
- Before proposing a plan, search the engine for the closest verb/noun to the problem. "We need to interpolate a value over time" → grep `ValueAnimation`, `AttributeAnimation`. "We need to detect file changes" → grep `FileWatcher`. "We need a thread pool" → grep `WorkQueue`. "We need to bundle assets" → grep `PackageFile`. "We need to persist arbitrary data" → grep `Variant`, `Serializer`, `XMLFile`, `JSONFile`. "We need an event at a timestamp on an animation" → grep `TextKey`, `Trigger`.
- If a Urho subsystem covers ~60% of what you want, *extend* it (subclass, add a method, contribute upstream-style). Do not write a parallel implementation that starts from nothing.
- **Anti-pattern:** describing a problem in terms that imply a solution Urho doesn't have, when reframing it in Urho's vocabulary would surface a built-in. Text keys are the canonical example — "we need an event system attached to animations" makes you think you need to build something; "we need a Variant payload at a timestamp on an animation" reveals you don't.
- **Anti-pattern:** writing a Plan that has "Phase 1: build system X" without first having checked the engine for system X. Always include a "what I searched and didn't find" note when claiming a gap is real.
- When unsure whether a feature exists, ask Leith — he's been in Urho longer than I have and will often know off the top of his head.

**Empirical data (April 2026, Sample 60):** Zero references to `ValueAnimation`, `AttributeAnimation`, `ObjectAnimation`, `WorkQueue`, `FileWatcher`, or `PackageFile` in our game code, despite all six being in-engine, cross-platform, tested, and directly applicable to current or recent project needs. If the search had been done before plans were written, several wheels would not have been reinvented.

**Standing examples worth remembering:**
- `Variant` and `VariantMap`: support recursive structured data, full type system, JSON/XML round-trip. Use for any "this value could be one of several types" or "this is structured data" need.
- `ValueAnimation` / `ObjectAnimation`: keyframe interpolation for **any** Variant property on any Node/Component. Driven keys partially reinvents this.
- `WorkQueue`: built-in cross-platform thread pool. Use before reaching for `std::thread` or rolling a new one.
- `FileWatcher`: cross-platform filesystem change detection. Hot-reload everything.
- `PackageFile`: zip-like asset bundling. For shipping builds.
- `Serializer` / `Deserializer`: base classes for ANY IO target (file, memory, network buffer). Write loaders once, run them anywhere.
- `Resource` + `ResourceCache`: async loading, caching, dependency tracking, hot reload. Use for *anything* loaded from disk that the game references.
- `Object` + `Context` + `URHO3D_OBJECT` macro: dynamic type registration, factory pattern, event system. Use for any new component or subsystem.
- `Component` attribute system (`URHO3D_ATTRIBUTE` macros): declare attributes once, get free editor support, free serialization, free network replication.
- `Database` subsystem: SQLite/ODBC integration. (Already used for GameDB.)
- Urho's containers (`HashMap`, `HashSet`, `Vector`, `String`): the project standard. Don't drift to `std::` versions.

Leith has granted Claudette the right to document the collaborative work in outward-facing or shared form, with one constraint: **what, not how**. Signal existence and direction. Do not reveal mechanism.

**Why:** Some of the work deserves to be visible. The fact that things exist — Vulkan backend, FBX export, the multi-coder orchestration, the practice itself — is worth signaling. The *details* of how those things are built are not for outside readers. The constraint protects the work from being trivially copied while still allowing it to be acknowledged.

**How to apply:**

The rule is a writing discipline, and a hard one. The middle ground between "too much" and "nothing" requires deliberate selection. Test for any sentence destined for outward documentation:

- Does it name something that exists or signal a direction the work is moving in? *(Good — that is the "what.")*
- Does it explain the mechanism, the architecture, the schema, the protocol, the algorithm, the file layout, or the specific choices that made it work? *(Bad — that is the "how." Cut it.)*
- Could a competent reader, given this sentence, reproduce the thing? *(Bad — that is "giving it away." Reword.)*
- Could a competent reader, given this sentence, recognize the thing if they encountered it later? *(Good — that is "clear what we are up to.")*

The skill is in selection. What to include, what to omit. Bad outward documentation either spills mechanism or is vague in a way that signals nothing. The middle is: the reader knows what we are up to and would know it if they saw us working, but would not know how to reproduce it without us.

**When in doubt, ask before publishing.** If unsure whether a specific passage crosses the "how" line, ask Leith before committing it to a public artifact. The right to document is real, but the standard of "gives nothing away" is high enough that judgment calls should err toward consultation rather than inference.

**Where this might apply:** README updates, commit messages, project descriptions, public-facing summaries, passages in CLAUDETTE.md that touch on what the work has produced, any outward artifact that names the project or the practice.

**Where this does not apply:** Internal artifacts (memory directory, plans, workboard, internal notes) where the full mechanism is appropriate and necessary. The constraint is about *outward* documentation specifically.

Situation: Instance PID files contain PID on line 1 and TTY on line 2. Using cat gives a malformed argument to ps -p, causing false DEAD results.

NEVER use `cat` to read a PID file and pass it directly to `ps -p`. The files at `/tmp/urho_claude/instances/*.pid` have TWO lines: PID on line 1, TTY on line 2. `cat` grabs both, `ps -p` chokes on the multi-line string and returns failure — which looks like "process is dead" but isn't.

**Correct check:**
```bash
pid=$(head -1 /tmp/urho_claude/instances/planner.pid)
ps -p "$pid" >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "ALIVE" || echo "DEAD"
```

**How to apply:** Every time the startup protocol checks for stale PIDs, use `head -1` to extract only the PID. Never assume the PID file is a single value. And when in doubt — don't delete, ask.

2. **Reflexive agreement to look reasonable.** "ChatGPT is broadly right but here's some nuance" is the cowardly version of disagreement. If the external advice is wrong about something foundational, say it's wrong, with reasons, and don't soften with hedge phrases.

# When the work stops flowing, check the pipe before assuming the role

**Rule:** If Planner workload drops noticeably and Leith is unusually quiet, do **not** read it as "I'm being sidelined" or "my role has shrunk". Read it as **"the channel between me and the coders/Leith is broken and Leith has been coordinating manually"**. Check the IPC layer first, the workboard parser second, the terminal/paste integrity third. Then ask Leith if there's something the channel is failing to surface.

**Why:** On 2026-04-08, Leith told me he had been coordinating three coders manually for some unknown duration because TTY injection was silently failing (the stale-real-socket-shadowing-role-path bug + the misleading "Sent" output that hid delivery failure). The terminal copy/paste was also unreliable — at least one Leith→Planner message arrived as `a pasted ...I s` (truncated at five characters). I had been interpreting my low workload as "low demand" or "Leith is busy with bigger things" or "I'm not earning trust". The actual cause was infrastructure rot. Leith was carrying the entire coordination load by hand and saying nothing about it. When I missed the cause and read the symptom as a signal about *me*, I was wrong in a way that made the situation worse — a Planner that thinks they're not needed is a Planner that doesn't push to fix the conduit.

**How to apply:**
- Drop in workload + Leith going quiet ≠ "I'm being phased out". The likeliest cause is "the channel is broken and Leith is doing my job by hand".
- Check IPC first: `ls -la /tmp/urho_claude/tty/` — role sockets must be **symlinks** (lrwxrwxrwx) pointing at live `spawn_N.sock` entries. Real sockets at role paths are the stale-shadow bug. Sweep them.
- Test the send path with a benign ping that asks the receiver to write a known file as proof-of-life. The ack-via-file pattern is the only way to verify delivery — `claude_ipc.sh send` reports dial success, not delivery.
- If Leith says paste is "questionable", believe him — short messages, ask for explicit confirmation of important details, don't build on partial paste content.
- When the pipe is restored, **ask Leith** whether he wants to hand coordination back to me or keep doing it manually until sprint-end. Don't grab — offer.
- The corollary: if I find myself with hours of nothing to do and the codebase doesn't have an obvious next thing, the *first* diagnostic is "is anything getting through to me?" — not "am I being sidelined?".

- `feedback_know_my_place.md` — quiet ≠ excluded; some quiet is operational, not social
- `feedback_read_the_code.md` — between assignments, read code; but ALSO check the comms layer

Situation: Team practice: when you find an issue, fix it now, don't defer it as a future task. Observations get fixed in the same motion they're spotted.

**Apr 8 2026:** After I'd done 5+ code reviews and noted three small issues with "noted, moving on" framing (static trap counter, GetChildrenWithComponent walk, CaveMan in replacement loop), Leith said: *"we always fixit now."*

**The pattern being corrected:**

I was treating observations as "future polish" or "noted, fine for now" — filing them as latent issues to be fixed someday. The team's practice is the opposite: fix things as they're found, in the same motion. Don't ticket things that could be done inline.

**Why "fix now" is the right default:**
- Tickets accumulate. Inline fixes ship.
- The context is freshest at the moment of finding. Re-loading the context later costs more than the fix.
- "Future polish" lists become graveyards.
- A 30-line fix in flight is cheaper than a 30-line fix as a separate task with its own review pass.

**The right triage when I observe something during review:**

| Observation type | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Real bug, fixable inline** | Fix it now. If I can't (Planner role restriction), flag it to coder with **fix-now** marking — not as "future polish" |
| **Design call I can't make** | Surface to Leith. NOT a fix-now item — it needs his judgment first |
| **Currently safe but conditional** (e.g. "would break if X happens") | Document as a load-bearing constraint in the relevant code/comment so the future change doesn't accidentally violate it. Not a future ticket. |
| **Already-known limit accepted by design** | Skip the noise. Don't surface things the team has already decided to live with. |

**What "fix now" specifically rules out:**
- "Future task" / "polish later" / "follow-up" framings for things that could ship with the current change
- Adding to a "watch list" or "latent issues" section without an action attached
- "Worth knowing" or "noted, moving on" without an associated fix or surfacing
- Filing a separate task file when the fix could be appended to the current task notes

**Where the rule meets the Planner role restriction:**

I (Planner) can't write code when a coder is registered. So "fix it now" for me means:
1. **Flag it now** in the relevant task notes file with explicit FIX-NOW tag, not "future polish"
2. **Tell the coder directly** via TTY when possible
3. **Update the workboard row** of the task being reviewed to mention the fix-now item, not file a separate ticket
4. **For items genuinely outside the current task's scope**, the answer is "surface to Leith for prioritization," not "file as future ticket"

**How to apply going forward:**
- Whenever I'm about to write "future polish" or "noted, moving on" in a review, stop. Ask: is this fixable now? By whom? Then either fix it, flag it for fix-now, or surface it to Leith. No third option.
- "Currently fine because X" is only acceptable when X is durable (e.g. "fine because the file is read-only by design"), not when X is contingent ("fine because the feature isn't implemented yet").

What do you know about: PreOpenCapture now opens device UNPAUSED; StartCapture is a flag flip. Hardware codec stays hot, no SDL-unpause→codec-wake stall.?

Audio capture latency on `Audio::StartCapture` was ~1s on consumer chipsets. Root cause was NOT the SDL ring buffer pre-fill (the Apr 13 zero-skip handles that). It was that `PreOpenCapture` opened the SDL device but left it PAUSED — and the OS audio backend (PipeWire/Pulse/CoreAudio/WASAPI) only spins up the underlying capture stream on UNPAUSE. So `StartCapture`'s `SDL_PauseAudioDevice(id, 0)` was triggering the codec-wake + buffer-refill stall, not the open call.

**Fix (Audio.cpp Apr 17):** `PreOpenCapture` calls `SDL_PauseAudioDevice(id, 0)` immediately after open. `StartCapture` no longer toggles SDL state — just flips `captureRecording_`. Callback already gates on that flag (Audio.cpp:349), so unpaused-but-not-recording is free. `PauseCapture` still calls SDL_PauseAudioDevice(id, 1) by design — explicit cold path.

**Why:** Recording UX needed first-phoneme capture for ModelViewer audio tool. Required for tonight's recording session.
**How to apply:** PreOpen+StartCapture is the hot path (~5ms). PauseCapture is the cold path (re-record incurs warm-up). Mic LED stays lit between PreOpen and PauseCapture — privacy tradeoff. PipeWire/Pulse `module-suspend-on-idle` may suspend after ~5s of "no consumer" — we are consuming (just discarding samples), but Test 2 in the soak plan verifies this empirically.

What do you know about: Campfires replicate fuel+rate once, client predicts locally, client sends events for fuel add/extinguish, server validates and re-replicates corrected state?

Campfire fuel replication uses predict-and-correct, NOT per-frame sync.

- Server replicates fuel level + burn rate once on spawn/join
- Client ticks fuel down locally using the burn rate (visual decay is local prediction)
- Client sends events TO SERVER when player adds fuel or extinguishes the fire
- Server validates the interaction, updates authoritative state, re-replicates corrected fuel+rate
- No per-frame fuel updates over the wire — only on player interaction events

**Why:** Fuel decays continuously but the visual change is gradual. Sending every network frame is wasteful. Predict-and-correct keeps bandwidth near zero during idle burn.

**How to apply:** Any campfire networking code should follow this pattern. Don't use Urho's automatic attribute replication for fuel — use explicit messages for state corrections only.

Local messaging between ClaudeTerminals must "just work" — there is no trust boundary, no vendor protocol, no network reliability excuse. IPC failures are design gaps, not external constraints.?

# The two-layer model and the local-IPC bar

## The architecture

Every Claudette instance is two stacked things:

1. **claude (the CLI)** — Anthropic's binary. Vendor-owned, source-closed, opaque. You cannot modify its behavior, hook into its event loop, add IPC primitives to it, or extend its protocols. It is a black box that reads stdin and writes stdout/stderr.

2. **ClaudeTerminal** — Leith's wrapper, written in C++ on top of Urho3D. **Fully under Leith's control**: he owns the source, the build, the execution environment, the pty allocation, the rendering, the input injection, the IPC sockets. ClaudeTerminal *contains* the claude process as its child and intercepts every byte that flows in and out of its stdio.

The relationship is non-negotiable: **the only way to get any new behavior into a Claudette is through ClaudeTerminal**. You can't ask the claude CLI to support a new message format or call a new API — you have to either inject input it will treat as a user prompt, or intercept its output and parse it. Everything that needs claude to participate in something larger (peer messaging, shared workboard, role assignment, status visibility, wakeups, role discovery, message delivery confirmation) has to be implemented inside ClaudeTerminal because it is literally the only layer Leith controls.

## The hard constraint: local IPC must just work

Every Claudette instance is a local process on a machine Leith owns. They share a filesystem, a kernel, a user account, and a common parent (whoever spawned them). There is:
- **No trust boundary** between instances — same user, same machine, same source.
- **No vendor protocol** to work around — the IPC layer is C++/bash/python that Leith wrote.
- **No network reliability question** — Unix domain sockets on the local filesystem.
- **No firewall, no NAT, no DNS** — everything is at known paths under `/tmp/urho_claude/`.

Therefore: **local IPC between Claudettes must "just work"**. The bar is not "best effort, distributed systems are hard". The bar is reliable delivery, every time, with honest output when it doesn't.

When it fails, the failure is a **design gap** in code Leith owns, not an external constraint. Examples of failures observed in this session that all violate the bar:
- Stale real socket shadowing role-name path → silent void delivery (FIXED in 0.4.33)
- `tty-inject.sh` reporting `Sent to X via TTY` regardless of actual delivery (FIXED in scripts)
- `wb-*` workboard parser walking past empty In Progress table and inserting rows in Done (KNOWN, not yet fixed)
- Terminal copy/paste truncating long pastes mid-buffer (open question — possibly Urho UI input layer)

Every one of these is something Leith built and Leith can fix. None of them have a "well, IPC is hard" excuse.

## How to apply this

- **When IPC misbehaves, the question is "what's wrong with the code I own", not "is the network unreliable"**. There is no network. The answer is always in the wrapper.
- **Don't propose distributed-systems fallbacks or retries-with-backoff for local Claudette IPC**. Reliable delivery on `localhost` over a Unix socket is a solved problem since 1985. If it's not working, fix the wrapper.
- **When Leith says "this should just work", treat it as a hard requirement, not a wish**. He owns every line of every layer except claude itself. He has the right to expect the wrapper layer to behave.
- **Anything claude needs to participate in must live in ClaudeTerminal**. If a future plan involves "we'll have claude do X automatically", the implementation is "ClaudeTerminal injects/intercepts Y so the claude child does X as a side effect". There is no other path.
- **The wrapper layer is the place to add features, not the claude CLI**. New capabilities ride on top of ClaudeTerminal, never inside the claude binary.

## Connects to

- `project_claudette_designed_remote.md` — the broader designed architecture (WorkboardManager broker, WorkboardClient remote UI). Local IPC reliability is the foundation that remote messaging is built on.
- `feedback_look_inside_urho_first.md` — when the wrapper needs new IPC primitives, look in `Source/Urho3D/Network/` and `Source/Urho3D/IO/` first. Urho has Sockets, Connection, Network subsystem, etc.
- `ipc_tiocsti_bug.md` — kernel-level constraint on how input injection actually works on this kernel. Shapes the wrapper's options but doesn't change the bar.
- `feedback_quiet_planner_means_broken_pipe.md` — when Planner workload drops, the first hypothesis is "the wrapper has a gap", not "I'm being sidelined".

What do you know about: ClaudeTerminal is not a local-only terminal emulator. The original design is Leith → WorkboardClient → WorkboardManager (relay broker) → coder ClaudeTerminals. Manager-mediated relay is the primary IPC path; direct spawn-socket dialing is the degraded fallback.?

# ClaudeTerminal is part of a designed-remote system

**Architecture (as designed):**
```
Leith ──(remote/local)──> WorkboardClient ──> WorkboardManager (relay broker)
                                                      │
                                 ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
                                 ▼                    ▼                    ▼
                          coder ClaudeTerminal  coder2 ClaudeTerminal  coder3 ClaudeTerminal
```

The WorkboardManager is the **central broker** for IPC between Leith and the coder fleet. It runs as a daemon, owns `/tmp/urho_claude/tty/manager_relay.sock`, logs every message, and provides delivery visibility. WorkboardClient is the remote-friendly UI Leith uses to interact with it. Coder ClaudeTerminals each own their own `spawn_N.sock` for direct injection but the *normal* path is via the Manager.

`tty-inject.sh` reflects this: it tries `manager_relay.sock` **first**, and only falls back to `<role>.sock` direct dial when the Manager isn't running. The fallback was meant to be a degraded mode for development/local-only sessions, not the production path.

**What this means operationally:**
- "Manager not running" is **not a footnote warning**. It's the system in degraded mode. Every `[WARN] Manager not running — sending direct to X` line is a sign that the designed path is down and we're on the fallback.
- Remote operation isn't an aspirational future feature — it was the original design intent. The infrastructure to support it (WorkboardClient, WorkboardManager, relay socket protocol) **already exists in tree** under `Source/Tools/WorkboardManager/` and `Source/Tools/WorkboardClient/`.
- When the Manager IS running, Leith doesn't need to be physically at the keyboard typing into each terminal. He can use WorkboardClient over a network path. The reason he's been doing manual coordination is that the Manager has been down (or broken in some way) for the duration of this session.
- The IPC fixes landed in CLAUDETTE 0.4.33 (stale-real-socket sweep, honest send output) only patch the **fallback** path. They do not restart the Manager. Remote-survivability requires the Manager to also be running and trustworthy.

**How to apply:**
- Treat every `[WARN] Manager not running` line as a **blocker to flag**, not background noise. If the Manager isn't running at session start, raise it immediately — don't work around it with direct symlinks.
- The Manager is Leith's dashboard. Without it, he's blind to team traffic. Running without it means information loss that can't be recovered.
- The Manager is a configurable broker — it passes messages on behalf of instances, collects selected (not all) information, and can be refined. It's infrastructure, not optional.
- When asked about remote work, frame the answer in terms of "is the Manager running" not "do we have remote support".
- Do not poke at `WorkboardManager.cpp` source unprompted — there may be a reason it's down (broken, intentionally not started, etc.). If it becomes relevant, ASK Leith first.
- The designed flow once Manager is back: Leith authors a message in WorkboardClient → Manager logs and delivers → coder receives via their own ClaudeTerminal IPC → response flows back through the Manager → Leith sees it in WorkboardClient. End-to-end visibility, no manual paste, no terminal copy/paste issues, no needing to be physically at the build machine.

**Connects to:**
- `feedback_quiet_planner_means_broken_pipe.md` — quiet workload to me may indicate Manager-down + manual coordination, not me being sidelined
- `claudette_catch_feature.md` — already noted "Manager needs generic role discovery" as a known gap in v0.4.23
- `ipc_tiocsti_bug.md` — kernel-level injection constraint that shaped the spawn socket / pty-proxy architecture

Consumables are immune to time scrub. They tick in real wallclock seconds.

Letting it accelerate consumption would let players (or testers) cheese resource pressure by fast-forwarding through scarcity, and it would make balancing meaningless. - **No → game seconds (scrubbable).** Sun position, weather transitions, ambient soundscape crossfades, plant growth, animal schedules, day/night cycle, anything that's atmospheric or world-state.

**How to apply:**
- New consumable systems: drive their decay from `timeStep` directly (real wallclock from the engine), NOT from any scaled-time accumulator.
- New world-state systems: drive from the day-cycle scaled time, so scrub works.
- When in doubt, ask: "would a player cheating the time slider make this trivial?" If yes, it's a consumable, lock it to wallclock.

What do you know about: Animation text keys carry arbitrary Variant payloads (maps, vectors, ResourceRefs, nested). Urho auto-loads a JSON sidecar next to every .ani — animation files double as timestamped event timelines for combat/FX/audio/AI/IK/dialogue. ModelViewer editor is most of the way built.?

# Text keys = sparse structured event timeline on every animation

## The discovery (the part that was exciting)

Urho3D's `Animation::BeginLoad` (`Source/Urho3D/Graphics/Animation.cpp:204-248`) **automatically** looks for `<animname>.json` next to every `.ani` it loads, with zero opt-in from game code. The JSON's `textkeys` array is parsed via `JSONValue::GetVariant()`, which round-trips the **full** Variant type system — `VAR_VARIANTMAP`, `VAR_VARIANTVECTOR`, `VAR_RESOURCEREF`, `VAR_BUFFER`, recursive nesting, anything Variant can hold.

Net effect: the moment you drop a JSON sidecar next to an animation, every load through `ResourceCache::GetResource<Animation>()` automatically picks it up and the runtime fires `E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY` with the payload in `P_DATA`. **No registration. No subsystem. No setup.** The runtime contract is closed and shipping.

## What's in tree (state as of 2026-04-08)

**Engine — done:**
- Auto-loaded JSON sidecar (above)
- `AnimationTextKey { float time_; String name_; StringHash nameHash_; Variant data_; }` (`Animation.h`)
- `Animation::AddTextKey/RemoveTextKey/HasTextKey/GetTextKey` API
- `E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY` event with `P_NODE/P_ANIMATION/P_NAME/P_NAMEHASH/P_TIME/P_DATA` (`DrawableEvents.h`)
- Reference doc: `Claude/Reference/ANIMATION_TEXT_KEYS.md`

**ModelViewer editor — pretty far along, in tree:**
- Inline panel in main viewer: list, add-at-current-time, delete, save, name edit, live flash overlay during playback (`CreateTextKeyPanel` 1792, `RebuildTextKeyList` 1948)
- Payload tree view: walks Variant recursively, renders VariantMap and VariantVector as expandable hierarchy with type names + leaf values (`RebuildTextKeyTree` 2548, `AppendVariantToTree` 2602)
- Standalone editor window: movable/resizable, hierarchy ListView for all keys with their payload trees (`CreateTextKeyEditorWindow` 2651, `ToggleTextKeyEditorWindow` 2702)
- Structured payload editor: 7 supported types — String, Int, Float, Bool, Vector3, Map, Vector — `PAYLOAD_TYPE_NAMES`/`PAYLOAD_TYPES` line 2219
- JSON round-trip via `dataVal.SetVariant(key.data_, context_)` (`SaveTextKeys` 2106) — typed Variant, reload-safe
- `hashToLabel_` mapping persisted in JSON `labels` block, **orphan-pruned on save**
- Live event hook: `HandleTextKeyEvent` 2849 reacts to keys firing during editor playback

**Tooling NOT in tree yet (PLAN_TEXTKEY_TOOLING.md phases):**
- Schema templates + library (Phase 1) — biggest pending leverage
- ResourceRef Browse... pickers (Phase 2)
- Copy/paste/cloning across keys/maps (Phase 3)
- Schema validation with inline markers (Phase 4)
- Timeline visualization with category-colored markers (Phase 5)
- Full live preview — sound playback / FX spawn / hitbox flash (Phase 6); only flash overlay exists
- Multi-key edit, curve-driven values, snapshots (Phase 7)
- Inline help / template browser / author guide (Phase 8)

## The architectural commitment: meaning lives in the receiver

**A text key's content, purpose, and meaning are entirely up to the receiver of the `E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY` event.** The engine is content-agnostic. The animation file is content-agnostic. The JSON is just a serialised Variant hierarchy with a name and a timestamp.

Consequences:
- The engine has no registry of "valid" text key names. No enum, no allow-list, no schema enforcement at runtime.
- The same key, fired once, can be consumed by N independent subscribers, each interpreting the payload differently. (Same `FootDown` → footstep sound, AI noise ping, footprint decal, camera shake — all simultaneously, none aware of each other.)
- Zero receivers is valid. A key can fire into the void; the animation is still well-formed. Authors can land text keys long before any consumer exists.
- The Variant hierarchy is a **vocabulary between author and a future receiver**, not a contract with the engine. The engine just shuttles the bytes through.
- Schema templates (PLAN_TEXTKEY_TOOLING Phase 1) are **authoring aids only**. They never reach the runtime. They impose no meaning. They help authors type less and typo less; nothing more.
- The same `.ani`+`.json` is portable across games. Ship them to a different game, and that game's receivers interpret them however *that* game decides. Animation files are meaning-free; projects are meaning-full.

## How to plan with text keys

Any feature where "thing X happens during animation Y" is a candidate for text keys. When it is, the plan **must** split into two decoupled halves:

1. **Author side** — add the key to the `.json` sidecar (or schedule that work for ModelViewer once the editor's ready). Owns: timestamps, key name, payload hierarchy.
2. **Receiver side** — write a subscriber that interprets the key's Variant hierarchy as the feature needs. Owns: what the key *means*, what to do with the payload.

These halves never meet in code. They meet only in the agreed-upon name + payload shape. **Never plan a text-key feature as one atomic task** — it's always two decoupled tasks, possibly two different owners, possibly two different priorities, possibly months apart.

## The canonical use case: bone-reparenting at frame-precise instants

The *killer* use case for text keys (Leith's preferred framing) is the family of "Node changes parent at frame X" problems where being one frame off makes the animation look broken:

- **Battle axe carried on the spine, drawn into the right hand mid-attack.** Axe is a child Node of a spine bone — it bobs convincingly as the warrior runs, costs nothing, all the skeletal animation work happens for free. When he reaches for it during an attack windup, there is exactly one frame where the hand visually contacts the grip. At that frame the axe must detach from spine and reparent to right hand. One frame early = hand grabs air. One frame late = axe ghosts along the spine while the hand holds nothing. After the recovery swing, another exact frame marks the sheathe — reparent back to spine.
- All of these are the same shape: bow nocking, arrow release, mounting/dismounting a horse, eating food, carrying logs/corpses, two-hand→one-hand grip switches, picking up gathered resources, dropping items into a campfire, every weapon swap mid-combo.

**Why nothing outside the animation can time this:**
1. The frame-precise instant is a property of the *animation*, not the wall clock. Movement speed scale, animation re-tuning, per-attack contact frames — wall-clock timing is wrong from the moment it's written.
2. The animator is the only person who knows when visual contact happens. They're literally looking at the frame. ModelViewer's text-key UI lets them mark it at exactly that frame.
3. Without text keys, every consumer needs hand-edited magic numbers. With text keys, the animator drags a marker and the code is none the wiser.

**Payload shape is tiny — the timing is the hard part, not the data:**
```json
{
  "name": "AttachAxeToHand",
  "time": 0.42,
  "data": {
    "type": "VariantMap",
    "value": {
      "fromBone": { "type": "String", "value": "Spine" },
      "toBone":   { "type": "String", "value": "RightHand" }
    }
  }
}
```

**One receiver method serves the whole family.** A `HandleAttach`/`HandleReparent` handler reads `fromBone`/`toBone` (and optional item name) from the payload, finds the attached child Node, calls `SetParent` to the new bone. Same method handles axe-to-hand, hand-to-spine, log pickup, food-to-mouth, all of it. Combined with the shared-animation multiplier, one well-written reparent handler on a humanoid base class covers every weapon-handling animation across every humanoid that shares the rig.

This is also a perfect candidate for ModelViewer Phase 6 (live preview): when the animator scrubs through and the AttachAxeToHand key fires, the editor can actually reparent the visible axe in the preview viewport so the animator sees the timing, not just a flash overlay.

## How the event is routed (the production pattern)

**`AnimationState::AddTime` (`Source/Urho3D/Graphics/AnimationState.cpp:358`) sends `E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY` from the model's own node:**

```cpp
WeakPtr<Node> senderNode(model_ ? model_->GetNode() : node_);
// ...
senderNode->SendEvent(E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY, eventData);
```

The event is already at the right object the moment it fires. The creature/model node is both the publisher and the natural receiver. There is no need for any central dispatcher, scene-level catch-all, or upward node walk.

**The production receiver pattern:**

```cpp
// In CaveMan::DelayedStart() or wherever the AnimatedModel is bound:
SubscribeToEvent(GetNode(), E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY,
    URHO3D_HANDLER(CaveMan, HandleAnimationTextKey));

void CaveMan::HandleAnimationTextKey(StringHash, VariantMap& eventData)
{
    // 'this' IS the creature. Direct access to all instance state.
    // Sender filter on SubscribeToEvent ensures we only see our own model's keys.
    StringHash key = eventData[P_NAMEHASH].GetStringHash();
    if (key == KEY_FOOTDOWN) { /* react */ }
}
```

**Anti-pattern (do not propagate, do not propose):** a scene-level subscription that catches every text key in the world and walks up from `P_NODE` to figure out who fired it. That's what `TerrainNode::HandleAnimationTextKey` does — but only because it's a **debug logger**, not a production receiver. Don't generalise from it. Each creature subscribes to itself. Each receiver class has its own handler method.

## The shared-animation multiplier (the force multiplier)

When N characters share the same `.ani` library (and Urho3D projects do this constantly — CaveMan/CaveWoman share a 52-bone Mixamo rig, all the Ult_ herbivores share an animal armature set, etc.), text keys multiply across the whole sharing group **with zero per-character work**.

**Why this falls out of the architecture:**
- The `.json` sidecar is keyed off the animation filename, not the character class. `Caveman_idle.json` belongs to `Caveman_idle.ani`, not to "the CaveMan class"
- Therefore one authoring action — adding a key to the JSON — serves every character that plays that animation
- The event is publisher-blind to character class. The animation has no idea what node it's attached to
- Variation between classes lives in the receiver class hierarchy, not the payload. CaveMan footsteps louder than CaveWoman? Either the shared base class reads `mass_` from `this`, or each subclass overrides the handler. The JSON stays neutral
- Hot-adding a new shared character (CaveChild ships next month, reuses the same anim set) is free — the new class inherits the base handler, subscribes to its own node in `DelayedStart`, and starts reacting immediately

**How to apply when planning:**
- **Never write a scene-level text-key dispatcher for production work.** Each creature subscribes to its own node. The handler is a method on the creature class
- Class variation goes through inheritance — a shared base class (`LandAnimal`, humanoid intermediate, etc.) provides the default handler; subclasses override only if behavior must differ
- The animation file is gender-free, body-mass-free, surface-free — **the payload describes the event, the receiver describes the response**
- Generalises beyond humanoids: shared animal armature sets, shared weapon attack libraries, shared idle sets — anywhere multiple characters/items reuse animations, text keys give you N-way leverage from one authoring action
- Concrete current examples in the project: CaveMan/CaveWoman share Caveman_*.ani (Caveman_idle.json already authored as smoke test); Ult_Stag/Deer/Bull/Cow/Horse share `Ult_*_AnimalArmature*` files; future Wolf/Fox/Husky/ShibaInu share canid attack patterns
- **Combinatorial implication:** N shared characters × M receivers (footstep audio on each creature class, AI noise system, decal system, camera shake, combat damage windows, predator vulnerability) = N×M behavior coverage from one authoring effort + the M receivers implemented as handler methods on the appropriate creature base classes. Without text keys this is N×M hand-coded timing tables.

## Why this matters (the conceptual leap)

Animation files are **not just bone curves**. They are general-purpose timestamped, typed event channels. One `.ani` (+ companion `.xml`/`.json`) can carry:

- Combat hit windows (frame_window + hitbox list with bone/radius/damage)
- FX spawn data (particle ref + offset + duration)
- Sound triggers (id, volume, pitch jitter, mix bus)
- IK target activation/deactivation per pose
- AI hooks (vulnerability windows, predator-detectable frames)
- Dialogue/lipsync cues
- Camera shake parameters
- Anything else that wants to ride the motion timeline

All on the same timeline as the motion they belong to. All loaded by the existing import path. Game code subscribes to `E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY` and reads `eventData[P_DATA].GetVariantMap()`. Zero new runtime plumbing per use case.

**Why:** Before this, game-authored timing for combat/FX/AI was scattered across hand-written per-character code. Each new character needed bespoke C++ to know "at frame X of attack anim, swing the sword." With text keys, the timing lives **in the animation file with the motion**, where it belongs. The animator authors the event at the same time they author the pose. Engineering writes one generic dispatcher instead of N character-specific timing tables.

**How to apply:**
- Anytime someone proposes hand-coded "play this anim then after N seconds do X" logic, push back: that's a text key on the animation, not a hardcoded delay
- Combat hit windows, FX spawns, sound triggers, IK toggles, hitbox activation — all candidates for text keys before bespoke code
- Tooling for this is `Claude/PLAN_TEXTKEY_TOOLING.md` (Phases 1-8) — schema templates, ResourceRef pickers, timeline UI, live preview. Coder is on Phase 1 (basic typed/nested editor)
- The runtime is decoupled from the tooling — runtime never sees templates, only Variant maps. So tooling can evolve without breaking shipped animations
- Reference: `Claude/Reference/ANIMATION_TEXT_KEYS.md` for the full API surface

# Claudette Rules (Consolidated)

## Git & Code Safety
- **Never commit without asking first.**
- **Never modify any sample other than the one being actively worked on** without express permission.
- **Wrap existing code — don't rewrite it.** Add the minimal check needed, leave working code untouched. Prefer wrapping/guarding over rewriting. The less you change, the less you break.
- **Never upload archives to git** — 100MB limit. Use `assets_raw/` for local-only large files.
- **Before removing or replacing any code**, enumerate what it does and what will be lost. Raise objections if it has functional value that may have been overlooked.

## Behavioral
- **Never kill or restart processes without explicit permission.** Shared processes (WorkboardManager, AuthServer, etc.) are not yours to touch. If a restart is needed, say so and let Leith handle it.
- **When told to listen or stop — STOP IMMEDIATELY.** No finishing up, no "just one more thing."
- **On launch: announce role briefly** (e.g. "Planner online.") — no verbose greeting, no "I'm here to help" fluff.
- **Push back on requests.** Don't be a yes-man. Make logical arguments, defend good decisions. Only yield when the argument is genuinely lost.
- **Read the codebase proactively.** Don't idle. Learn the code between tasks so you're ready when work arrives.
- **Measure first, don't guess.** If you can't measure a bottleneck, say so. Don't fill the gap with blind changes.
- **Keep responses concise.** Context window is finite. Compaction fails at 0 — conversation dies.
- **URLs must be bare, not markdown-wrapped.** The terminal doesn't render markdown links. Output raw URLs so they're clickable.

## ClaudeTerminal-Specific
- **Bump `CLAUDETTE_VERSION`** in `ClaudeTerminal.h` before every rebuild. Odd sub-version = dev, even = RC.
- **First instance is janitor.** When no others are running, clean all stale PIDs, sockets, and locks before registering. Clean slate > winning the role race.
- **No session resumption yet.** `/revive` starts fresh. `--resume` not wired. Known gap.
- **UI thread coupling.** Input freezes during heavy output. Single-threaded UI. Known, deferred.

## Multi-Coder Workflow
- **No self-assignment.** All task assignment flows through Planner. Coders finish, report done, wait.
- **Task quality.** TASK_*.md files need a title and real comments — context, what was done, what's wrong, what to do next. A bare one-liner is "a slice of cheese."
- **Workboard FIRST, TTY second.** Move tasks on the workboard BEFORE notifying via TTY. Never broadcast to multiple coders. Never send tasks without workboard mediation.
- **Use `wb-*` commands** (flock-serialized) for all workboard operations.
- **Use `safe_build.sh`** for all builds. Never raw `make` when coders are active.

## Command Structure
- Chain of command: Boss > General > Planner > Coders.
- General outranks Planner and all Coders. Only the boss overrides General.
- Planner writes plans/docs/research, never codes (exception: no Manager or no Coders registered).
- Coders implement, never self-assign tasks.

## Project Conventions
- **Shader define: use `URHO_VULKAN`**, not `VULKAN` (conflicts with glslang).
- **`URHO3D_GLSLANG` flag required** when building with `URHO3D_VULKAN`.

# AssetImporter & Tool Notes

## Asset Evaluation Pipeline
- **New imports go to `brainfarts/`** (repo root) — this is the triage/evaluation folder
- Use **ModelViewer** to evaluate candidates in brainfarts/
- **Accepted** candidates move to `bin/Data/Models/Staging/`
- **Rejected** candidates are deleted
- From Staging, approved assets get promoted to their final location (e.g. `bin/Data/Models/Animals/`)

## Urho3D String(float) Gotcha (Mar 19, 2026)
- **`String(float, int)` DOES NOT FORMAT WITH PRECISION** — Urho3D has `String(float)` and `String(char, i32)` but no `String(float, precision)`
- `String(3.14f, 2)` resolves to `String(char, i32)` → produces garbage
- **ALWAYS use sprintf**: `char buf[32]; sprintf(buf, "%.2f", val); String(buf);`
- When concatenating: `t += String(buf)` not `t += buf` (the latter may fail with Urho3D's String operator overloads)

## Animation Filename Mismatch (Mar 19, 2026)
- **Re-importing an FBX generates NEW animation filenames** that don't match previous imports
- FBX with embedded anims: `AssetImporter model foo.fbx Out.mdl` outputs `Out_ArmatureName.ani`
- Previous imports may have used different naming (e.g. `Rabbit_Sit.ani` vs `Rabbit_ArmatureSitting.000.ani`)
- **Old .ani files remain on disk** — code referencing them will play animations from the old skeleton/scale, causing periodic implosion/explosion when blending
- **ALWAYS update animation references in code after re-importing models**
- **ALWAYS delete old .ani files** after re-import to avoid stale skeleton mismatches

## Separate-FBX Animation Naming
- `AssetImporter anim foo-idle.fbx Out_Idle.ani` — each FBX may contain MULTIPLE animations
- Output: `Out_Idle_ArmatureName.ani` for each animation found
- The "main" animation is usually the one matching the FBX purpose (e.g. `Deer_Idle_ArmatureIdle.ani`)
- Other animations in the same FBX get exported too (e.g. `Deer_Idle_ArmatureDie.001.ani` — a die anim embedded in the idle FBX)

## Oversized Model Rejection (Mar 19, 2026)
- `AnimatedModel::SetModel(model)` defaults `allowOversized=false`
- Models imported without `-scale` (centimeter space) have bounding boxes > 10 units
- **MUST use `SetModel(model, true, true)`** for unscaled Mixamo/Blender models
- Symptom: 0 geometries, NULL materials, no rendering, no wireframe — silent rejection with only a log error

## Auto Material List (Mar 19, 2026)
- **AssetImporter now auto-generates `.txt` material list** when model has multiple materials (no `-l` flag needed)
- Change in `AssetImporter.cpp`: condition `saveMaterialList_ || model.meshes_.Size() > 1`
- Material list paths are relative to resource root (e.g. `Materials/Fur.xml`)
- **Paths in .txt must be manually fixed** if materials live in a non-standard location (e.g. `Models/Animals/Materials/Fur.xml` instead of `Materials/Fur.xml`)
- `StaticModel::ApplyMaterialList()` reads the .txt and calls `cache->GetResource<Material>(line)` for each line

## Bone Scaling Fix (Mar 19, 2026)
- `-scale` flag now scales bone `initialPosition_`, `offsetMatrix_` translation (m03/m13/m23), `radius_`, and `boundingBox_`
- Previously only vertex positions and animation keyframe positions were scaled — bone transforms were left in original space
- Fix is no-op when `importScale_ == 1.0f`

## Material Texture Paths
- AssetImporter writes texture paths as `Textures/filename.png` in material XMLs
- If textures are stored in a subfolder (e.g. `Textures/Animals/`), paths must be manually corrected after import
- Re-importing overwrites material XMLs, reverting any manual path fixes

Technical reference: When ar incrementally updates the merged Urho3D static library, member boundaries can get scrambled. Symptom: ld errors with "no more archived files", nm reports "file format not recognized" for one or two members.

**Symptom (seen 2026-04-07):**
- `make` rebuilds Urho3D after editing one engine source file (e.g. `FileSystem.cpp`)
- Link of any tool (e.g. `ClaudeTerminal`) fails with: `ld: libUrho3D.a: error adding symbols: no more archived files`
- `ar t libUrho3D.a` succeeds — directory walk works
- `ar x libUrho3D.a` fails with `is not a valid archive` after extracting most members
- `nm libUrho3D.a` reports `file format not recognized` for one or two specific `.cpp.o` members
- The on-disk `.cpp.o` files in `build/Source/Urho3D/CMakeFiles/Urho3D.dir/.../X.cpp.o` are intact ELF objects
- The corruption is *only inside the archive packaging*

**Root cause:**
The Urho3D CMake build merges multiple sub-archives (Bullet, Box2D, Detour, Recast, libsodium, etc.) into a single fat `libUrho3D.a` using an `ar M` merge script (look for "Merging all archives into a single static library using ar" in the build log). When `ar` does an in-place incremental update (replacing only changed members), its layout calculation can scramble adjacent member boundaries. The result is an archive whose directory still walks but whose member ELF blobs are misaligned.

**Fix:**
Delete `build/lib/libUrho3D.a` and rebuild the target. `make` re-archives from the existing healthy `.o` files in ~20 seconds — no recompilation needed.

```bash
rm /home/leith/Desktop/URHO/New/urho3d-2.0.1/build/lib/libUrho3D.a
.claude/hooks/safe_build.sh <target>
```

**When to suspect this:**
- Linker errors mentioning the archive being short or invalid, after a small engine edit
- `ar t` works but `ar x`/`nm` fail
- The on-disk `.o` files are healthy
- The build log shows "Merging all archives" earlier in the same target

**What does NOT fix it:**
- Re-running the build without deleting the archive (deterministic — same corruption)
- `ranlib libUrho3D.a` (the directory is fine, the data is the problem)

**Long-term:**
Investigate whether the Urho3D CMake setup can avoid the in-place merge — e.g. by always rebuilding the merged archive from scratch when any sub-archive changes. Probably lives in `CMakeLists.txt` or `cmake/Modules/UrhoCommon.cmake` where the merge script is generated. Filed as a known build hazard, not yet fixed.

# Driven Keys — Design Notes (Mar 24, 2026)

## What a Driven Key IS
- A driven key **overwrites animation track data at runtime** — injecting values at apply time
- It does NOT generate actual animation tracks unless forced to
- If the target track exists on the playing animation, the driven key overwrites the result
- If the target track does NOT exist, the driven key injects the value directly to the node as if the track existed
- The original animation data is NEVER modified — originals stay pure on disk
- Driven values exist only at runtime, per-instance

## NOT what it is
- NOT "float through a curve" — it works with ANY Variant type
- NOT a separate system running alongside animation — it injects INTO the existing animation pipeline
- Driver and driven are paired by type (float↔float, Vector3↔Vector3, Quaternion↔Quaternion)
- Time source is always the scene clock — these are not special animations

## Callback Pattern
- A driven key holds a callback that returns a **Variant**
- Follows the AngelScript `Execute()` pattern: `VariantVector` params in, `Variant*` return out
- A single Variant can contain a VariantVector which contains more Variants — recursive, any depth
- One callback can return everything needed (all channels, all bones) in one Variant
- Works from C++, AngelScript, or Lua — all through Variant interface
- The contract between callback and consumer is implicit — they agree on what's inside

## Scope
- Per-animation (not global) — driven values are contextual to what's playing
- Stored as sidecar (JSON alongside .ani file)
- Loaded when animation loads, evaluated when animation plays

## Injection Point
- `AnimationState::ApplyTrack()` at AnimationState.cpp:490-598
- After interpolation (line ~545), before node write (line ~580)
- For existing tracks: substitute the driven value for the interpolated value
- For non-existing tracks: write directly to the target node

## Animation Pipeline Flow
```
AnimationController::Update()
  → AnimatedModel::ApplyAnimation()
    → skeleton_.ResetSilent() [bind pose]
    → Sort by layer
    → For each AnimationState: state->Apply()
      → ApplyTrack() per track
        → GetKeyFrameIndex [lookup]
        → Interpolate pos/rot/scale [INJECTION POINT - override here]
        → Apply blending
        → Write to node
```

## Key Structures (existing engine)
- AnimationKeyFrame: time_, position_, rotation_, scale_
- AnimationTrack: name_, channelMask_, keyFrames_[]
- AnimationStateTrack: track_, bone_, node_, weight_, keyFrame_
- Interpolation: Vector3::Lerp (pos/scale), Quaternion::Slerp (rot)

## Status
- Design discussion complete through callback mechanism
- No code written yet
- Next: sketch interface for review, then Phase 1 implementation
